mcqs.question: Why is creating a git branch nearly instant regardless of repository size?
options: A branch is a small pointer file holding a commit hash, not a copy of the project's files
Branches are only materialized on disk the first time you commit to them
Git creates a lightweight symlink to the working directory rather than copying anything
Git defers the actual branch creation until the next push
mcqs.explanation: Creating a branch just writes a 41-byte ref pointing at a commit hash; there's no proportional cost to repo size because no files are duplicated. It isn't a symlink, isn't deferred, and exists immediately, not just on first commit.

mcqs.question: What's the difference between `git branch -d feature` and `git branch -D feature`?
options: -d deletes only local branches, -D also deletes the matching remote branch
-d refuses to delete if the branch has unmerged commits, -D deletes regardless
-d renames the branch before deleting, -D deletes immediately
There is no functional difference; -D is simply the newer flag
mcqs.explanation: Lowercase -d is a safety check: it refuses to delete a branch whose commits aren't reachable elsewhere, preventing silent work loss. Uppercase -D forces deletion regardless. Neither touches remote branches or does any renaming.

mcqs.question: `main` hasn't gained any commits since `feature` branched off it. What happens when you run `git merge feature` from `main`?
options: Git creates a merge commit with two parents even though nothing conflicts
Git refuses to merge because the branches haven't diverged
Git performs a fast-forward, simply moving main's pointer to feature's tip with no new commit
Git squashes feature's commits into a single new commit on main
mcqs.explanation: When main is a strict ancestor of feature, there's nothing to reconcile, so git just slides the main pointer forward — a fast-forward, no merge commit created. A merge commit and squashing are both explicit alternate behaviors, not what happens by default here.

mcqs.question: Two branches both edited the same file, but on completely different lines. Why does git merge this automatically without a conflict?
options: Because git only checks for conflicts in the file's first and last lines
Because git compares each branch's changes against the shared merge base, and non-overlapping line changes apply cleanly from both sides
Because whichever branch has more commits automatically wins
Because git ignores line-level changes and only compares whole-file checksums
mcqs.explanation: A merge is a three-way diff against the common ancestor; if the two branches' changes don't touch the same lines, both sets apply cleanly with no ambiguity. Git doesn't pick a winner by commit count or only check edge lines, and it very much operates at line granularity, not whole-file checksums.

mcqs.question: In a merge conflict, what does the content between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======` represent?
options: The version from the branch being merged in
The version from your current branch (the one you're standing on)
The version from the shared merge base before either branch changed it
Whichever version git thinks is more likely correct
mcqs.explanation: The HEAD section is always your current branch's content; the section after ======= down to the second marker is the incoming branch's content. Git never guesses a "more correct" version, and the base version isn't shown at all in the default marker format.

mcqs.question: A team wants main's history to stay perfectly linear with no merge commits, and is willing to require branches to rebase before merging. Which merge mode enforces that?
options: git merge --no-ff
git merge --squash
git merge --ff-only
git merge -X ours
mcqs.explanation: --ff-only refuses anything but a fast-forward, erroring out and forcing a rebase first if main has diverged, which guarantees a linear history. --no-ff does the opposite (forces a merge commit), --squash produces one commit but doesn't require linearity beforehand, and -X ours is a conflict-resolution strategy, not a linearity guarantee.

mcqs.question: You're checked out on `feature` and accidentally run `git merge main` instead of merging feature into main. What actually happens?
options: Nothing changes since you specified the wrong direction
main's commits get merged into feature; main itself is untouched
feature's commits get merged into main automatically as a safeguard
Git detects the mistake and aborts before making any changes
mcqs.explanation: Merge direction is determined by which branch you're currently on — main flows into whatever you're standing on, here feature, leaving main untouched. Git has no built-in detection for "wrong direction" merges; it does exactly what you told it.

mcqs.question: A reviewer opens a PR and sees changes the author swears they never made. What's the most likely cause?
options: The reviewer is looking at the wrong pull request
The feature branch is far behind main, so the diff's stale merge base includes unrelated commits main gained since divergence
Git corrupted the PR's diff calculation
The author force-pushed and lost some commits
mcqs.explanation: PR diffs are computed against the current merge base; a branch that hasn't pulled main in a while has an old base, so main's unrelated intervening commits show up as if they were part of the PR. This isn't corruption or a wrong-PR mixup, and lost commits from a force-push would show as missing work, not extra unrelated diffs.
